chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Shamoun, from Abdullah ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Asam, from Misma' ibn Abd al-Malik, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) ruled regarding Al-Mamouma (skull fracture reaching the brain) as one-third of the blood money; and regarding Al-Munqila (bone-displacing injury) as fifteen camels; and regarding Al-Mudhiha (bone-exposing injury) as five camels; and regarding Al-Damiya (bloody injury) as one camel; and regarding Al-Bazi'a (flesh-exposing injury) as two camels. And he ruled regarding Al-Mutalahima (flesh injury) as three camels, and ruled regarding Al-Simhaq (injury reaching the bone) as four camels.

key_terms.الدِّيَة: Blood money or compensation for injury/death
key_terms.السِّمْحَاق: An injury that reaches the bone
key_terms.الْبَاضِعَة: An injury that exposes the flesh
key_terms.الْمَأْمُومَة: A fracture of the skull reaching the brain
key_terms.الْمُنَقِّلَة: An injury that displaces a bone from its joint
key_terms.الْمُوضِحَة: An injury that exposes the bone

ai.seo_question: What are the specific blood money amounts for different types of head and body injuries in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith, recorded in Al-Kafi, establishes the prophetic precedent for 'diyah' (blood money) by detailing specific compensation for distinct categories of head injuries, such as the 'Ma'mumah' (skull fracture) and 'Damiah' (bleeding wound). It highlights the precision of Shia jurisprudence in categorizing injuries based on depth and visibility, reflecting the practical application of Quranic principles of retribution and compensation. The narration underscores the continuity of legal authority from the Prophet through Imam Ali, reinforcing the legitimacy of Imami judicial rulings.
